query: What must a server include in a 405 Method Not Allowed response?

passages.heading: RFC 9110, section 15.5.6 (405 Method Not Allowed)
passages.text: The 405 (Method Not Allowed) status code indicates that the method received in the request-line is known by the origin server but not supported by the target resource. The origin server MUST generate an Allow header field in a 405 response containing a list of the target resource's currently supported methods.

query: How long should an OAuth 2.0 authorization code live, and can a client use it twice?

passages.heading: RFC 6749, section 4.1.2 (Authorization Response), code
passages.text: The authorization code MUST expire shortly after it is issued to mitigate the risk of leaks. A maximum authorization code lifetime of 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED. The client MUST NOT use the authorization code more than once. If an authorization code is used more than once, the authorization server MUST deny the request and SHOULD revoke (when possible) all tokens previously issued based on that authorization code.

query: What values can the Retry-After header take?

passages.heading: RFC 9110, section 10.2.3 (Retry-After)
passages.text:
The Retry-After field value can be either an HTTP-date or a number of seconds to delay after receiving the response.

A delay-seconds value is a non-negative decimal integer, representing time in seconds.

Two examples of its use are

Retry-After: Fri, 31 Dec 1999 23:59:59 GMT
Retry-After: 120

In the latter example, the delay is 2 minutes.

query: Does the Secure attribute stop an attacker on an insecure connection from overwriting a cookie?

passages.heading: RFC 6265, section 4.1.2.5 (The Secure Attribute)
passages.text:
The Secure attribute limits the scope of the cookie to "secure" channels (where "secure" is defined by the user agent). When a cookie has the Secure attribute, the user agent will include the cookie in an HTTP request only if the request is transmitted over a secure channel (typically HTTP over Transport Layer Security (TLS) [RFC2818]).

Although seemingly useful for protecting cookies from active network attackers, the Secure attribute protects only the cookie's confidentiality. An active network attacker can overwrite Secure cookies from an insecure channel, disrupting their integrity (see Section 8.6 for more details).

query: Which status code should a server return when a PUT creates a new resource, and which when it updates one?

passages.heading: RFC 9110, section 9.3.4 (PUT)
passages.text: If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response. If the target resource does have a current representation and that representation is successfully modified in accordance with the state of the enclosed representation, then the origin server MUST send either a 200 (OK) or a 204 (No Content) response to indicate successful completion of the request.

query: Is a JSON object with a duplicate key valid, and what will a parser do with it?

passages.heading: RFC 8259, section 4 (Objects)
passages.text:
The names within an object SHOULD be unique.

An object whose names are all unique is interoperable in the sense that all software implementations receiving that object will agree on the name-value mappings. When the names within an object are not unique, the behavior of software that receives such an object is unpredictable. Many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs, including duplicates.

query: How large can a WebSocket ping or close frame be, and can it be fragmented?

passages.heading: RFC 6455, section 5.5 (Control Frames)
passages.text: All control frames MUST have a payload length of 125 bytes or less and MUST NOT be fragmented.

query: An HTTP/1.1 message has both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length. Which one wins?

passages.heading: RFC 9112, section 6.3 (Message Body Length)
passages.text: If a message is received with both a Transfer-Encoding and a Content-Length header field, the Transfer-Encoding overrides the Content-Length. Such a message might indicate an attempt to perform request smuggling (Section 11.2) or response splitting (Section 11.1) and ought to be handled as an error. An intermediary that chooses to forward the message MUST first remove the received Content-Length field and process the Transfer-Encoding (as described below) prior to forwarding the message downstream.

query: Is TRUNCATE in PostgreSQL MVCC-safe, and can it be rolled back?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17, TRUNCATE, Notes
passages.text:
TRUNCATE is not MVCC-safe. After truncation, the table will appear empty to concurrent transactions, if they are using a snapshot taken before the truncation occurred. See Section 13.6 for more details.

TRUNCATE is transaction-safe with respect to the data in the tables: the truncation will be safely rolled back if the surrounding transaction does not commit.

query: What length limit does a PostgreSQL varchar column have if I declare it without a length?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17, 8.3 Character Types
passages.text: If character varying (or varchar) is used without length specifier, the type accepts strings of any length.

query: Can a PostgreSQL serial column have gaps even if no rows are deleted?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17, 8.1.4 Serial Types
passages.text: Because smallserial, serial and bigserial are implemented using sequences, there may be "holes" or gaps in the sequence of values which appears in the column, even if no rows are ever deleted. A value allocated from the sequence is still "used up" even if a row containing that value is never successfully inserted into the table column. This may happen, for example, if the inserting transaction rolls back.

query: What is PostgreSQL's default max_connections, and can it be changed without a restart?

passages.heading: PostgreSQL 17, 19.3.1 Connection Settings, max_connections
passages.text: Determines the maximum number of concurrent connections to the database server. The default is typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb). This parameter can only be set at server start.

query: Does SQLite have a boolean type?

passages.heading: SQLite, Datatypes In SQLite, 2.1 Boolean Datatype
passages.text:
SQLite does not have a separate Boolean storage class. Instead, Boolean values are stored as integers 0 (false) and 1 (true).

SQLite recognizes the keywords "TRUE" and "FALSE", as of version 3.23.0 (2018-04-02) but those keywords are really just alternative spellings for the integer literals 1 and 0 respectively.

query: Should I add AUTOINCREMENT to an SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY?

passages.heading: SQLite, AUTOINCREMENT, Summary
passages.text:
The AUTOINCREMENT keyword imposes extra CPU, memory, disk space, and disk I/O overhead and should be avoided if not strictly needed. It is usually not needed.

In SQLite, a column with type INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias for the ROWID (except in WITHOUT ROWID tables) which is always a 64-bit signed integer.

query: When does ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN fail in SQLite?

passages.heading: SQLite, ALTER TABLE, 5. ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN
passages.text:
The DROP COLUMN command only works if the column is not referenced by any other parts of the schema and is not a PRIMARY KEY and does not have a UNIQUE constraint. Possible reasons why the DROP COLUMN command can fail include:
The column is a PRIMARY KEY or part of one.
The column has a UNIQUE constraint.
The column is indexed.
The column is named in the WHERE clause of a partial index.
The column is named in a table or column CHECK constraint not associated with the column being dropped.
The column is used in a foreign key constraint.
The column is used in the expression of a generated column.
The column appears in a trigger or view.

query: What does -7 // 2 give in Python, and what type does 7 / 2 return?

passages.heading: Python 3, The Python Language Reference, 6.7 Binary arithmetic operations
passages.text: The / (division) and // (floor division) operators yield the quotient of their arguments. The numeric arguments are first converted to a common type. Division of integers yields a float, while floor division of integers results in an integer; the result is that of mathematical division with the 'floor' function applied to the result. Division by zero raises the ZeroDivisionError exception.

query: What does Python's str.split() do with several spaces in a row when no separator is given?

passages.heading: Python 3, Built-in Types, str.split
passages.text: If sep is not specified or is None, a different splitting algorithm is applied: runs of consecutive whitespace are regarded as a single separator, and the result will contain no empty strings at the start or end if the string has leading or trailing whitespace. Consequently, splitting an empty string or a string consisting of just whitespace with a None separator returns [].

query: Is Python's sort stable?

passages.heading: Python 3, Sorting Techniques, Sort Stability and Complex Sorts
passages.text: Sorts are guaranteed to be stable. That means that when multiple records have the same key, their original order is preserved.

query: Why does [80, 9].sort() in JavaScript put 80 first?

passages.heading: MDN, Array.prototype.sort(), Description
passages.text: If compareFn is not supplied, all non-undefined array elements are sorted by converting them to strings and comparing strings in UTF-16 code units order. For example, "banana" comes before "cherry". In a numeric sort, 9 comes before 80, but because numbers are converted to strings, "80" comes before "9" in the Unicode order. All undefined elements are sorted to the end of the array.

passages.heading: MDN, typeof, typeof null

query: In Go, when are a deferred call's arguments evaluated, and in what order do deferred calls run?

passages.heading: The Go Programming Language Specification, Defer statements
passages.text: Each time a "defer" statement executes, the function value and parameters to the call are evaluated as usual and saved anew but the actual function is not invoked. Instead, deferred functions are invoked immediately before the surrounding function returns, in the reverse order they were deferred.

query: Does Go's append always copy the slice into a new array?

passages.heading: The Go Programming Language Specification, Appending to and copying slices
passages.text: If the capacity of s is not large enough to fit the additional values, append allocates a new, sufficiently large underlying array that fits both the existing slice elements and the additional values. Otherwise, append re-uses the underlying array.

query: Can I get the first character of a Rust String with s[0]?

passages.heading: The Rust Programming Language, 8.2 Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings, Indexing into Strings
passages.text:
The error tells the story: Rust strings don't support indexing. But why not? To answer that question, we need to discuss how Rust stores strings in memory.

A String is a wrapper over a Vec<u8>.

query: How long does Kubernetes wait by default before force-killing a Pod that is being deleted?

passages.heading: Kubernetes, Pod Lifecycle, Termination of Pods
passages.text:
By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The kubectl delete command supports the --grace-period=<seconds> option which allows you to override the default and specify your own value.

Setting the grace period to 0 forcibly and immediately deletes the Pod from the API server.

query: What type does a Kubernetes Service get if I don't set one, and can it be reached from outside the cluster?

passages.heading: Kubernetes, Service, Service type, ClusterIP
passages.text: Exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP. Choosing this value makes the Service only reachable from within the cluster. This is the default that is used if you don't explicitly specify a type for a Service. You can expose the Service to the public internet using an Ingress or a Gateway.

query: How much data can a Kubernetes ConfigMap hold?

passages.heading: Kubernetes, ConfigMaps
passages.text: A ConfigMap is not designed to hold large chunks of data. The data stored in a ConfigMap cannot exceed 1 MiB. If you need to store settings that are larger than this limit, you may want to consider mounting a volume or use a separate database or file service.

query: Why doesn't my container stop cleanly on docker stop when the Dockerfile uses ENTRYPOINT in shell form?

passages.heading: Dockerfile reference, ENTRYPOINT, Shell form ENTRYPOINT
passages.text: The shell form of ENTRYPOINT ignores any CMD or docker run command line arguments. It also starts your ENTRYPOINT as a subcommand of /bin/sh -c, which does not pass signals. This means that the executable will not be the container's PID 1, and will not receive Unix signals. In this case, your executable doesn't receive a SIGTERM from docker stop <container>.

query: What does Dockerfile ADD do with a local tar archive or a URL?

passages.heading: Dockerfile reference, ADD
passages.text:
If <src> is a local tar archive, it is decompressed and extracted to the specified destination. See Adding local tar archives.
If <src> is a URL, the contents of the URL are downloaded and placed at the specified destination. See Adding files from a URL.
If <src> is a Git repository, the repository is cloned to the specified destination. See Adding files from a Git repository.
